correctness.rationale: Checked the companion transition and initial state, M^13=I+3B, the four zero classes modulo 3, and the branch slopes (12,17,29,158). For j>=2 the coefficients of the falling-factorial polynomials in the normalized interpolation have valuation j−1−v3(j!)>=1 and tending to infinity. Their divided differences therefore give the claimed 1-Lipschitz remainder after extracting 3. This proves the constant class 0 from its unit constant and the three isometries from their unit slopes. The isometries are bijections on every finite residue ring and hence on the inverse limit, so the roots are unique and the valuation formula holds at every nonnegative index, including R_1=0. The base matrix has order 13 modulo 3, and cubing I+3^{j+1}U with U=B mod 3 increases the first nonzero matrix valuation by exactly one. This establishes order 13·3^{k−1}, not merely divisibility by this number. At k>=2 each isometry selects one t mod 3^{k−1}; k=1 instead has four base zeros. The classes for each exact valuation are differences of residue cylinders, giving the three asserted density cases. Independently followed basis-vector and Perrin-state orbits and checked all zero indices in a period through k=8, and separately confirmed the branch slopes and interpolation inputs.
residual_risks: Finite modular checks corroborate but do not establish the all-depth valuation theorem. The scope is the specified initial values, prime 3, and nonnegative indices.

evidence: For the transpose N of the frozen matrix, §1 gives N^13=I+3A with A nonzero mod 3. Since N is not identity mod 3, its reduced order is the prime 13. §3 gives (I+3A)^h≡I+3hA mod 3^{v3(h)+2}; this pins down exactly when a positive power of N^13 is identity mod 3^k. Its three root congruences then select one index each per such period at k>=2 and the base residue list gives four at k=1.
